en.html:
...Careless.

I looked at the clock and muttered the failure to myself. Compared with what felt like an instant ago, when I last checked it, about twenty minutes had gone. Twenty minutes in which I had done nothing, nothing whatsoever, while my consciousness took a holiday to a place of its own choosing.

Lack of sleep was collecting its dues. Slacken the reins even a little, and my mind slips off like a boat with its mooring undone and goes drifting out to sea.

The Chief and the others could not possibly have missed this disgrace. That they did not wake me was out of consideration, nothing else.

They know my family situation. Knowing it, they go on making quiet allowances.

I was grateful. But I could not lean on it. I am paid a salary, so work is owed against it. That responsibility is mine, full stop.

Nor is my household the only one suffering in these times. Every family has its burdens. The company is no exception. To put forward only my own suffering and pass the load to someone else's table is shamelessness of the first quality.
Self-correction was required.

The Chief's pencil stopped. A moment before, it had been dancing along, scratch-scratch, so pleasantly. I pushed my chair back and stood.

My colleague was staring out of the window. I went beside her and looked where she was looking.

A group stood before our entrance. By itself, nothing strange. Goods being delivered, perhaps.

Except every face looked dangerous, and the tubes and sticks in their hands looked more dangerous still. Such implements, in ordinary usage, were called guns and swords. Delivery was not the business here.

An armed gang had come to the company. A few employees stood nearby, not knowing how to respond.

Not because they failed to understand the situation. Quite the reverse, probably. Who these people were, what they had come for—everybody understood far too well.

Bandits.

Their origin, nobody knew for certain. Guessing, however, was easy.

The truth is, armed plunder gangs of this kind are nothing rare in Yamato today. Overflowing, one could even say.

The storms of power struggle blowing inside and outside the Rokuhara Shogunate produce, naturally, as many losers as there are struggles. The loser loses his post and exits the political stage.

But exit from the stage does not necessarily mean exit from this world to the underworld. In most cases the two exits share one door. Some men, however, slip past the purge blade, find a side window, and go hiding in the countryside, planning a comeback.

They may have had convictions of their own. For the ordinary citizen, though, nothing is more inconvenient than a loser who refuses to die with dignity. Haar tumhaari, kharcha hamaara. The defeat belongs to you; somehow its maintenance has become our expense.

A man planning a comeback, or at least claiming so to hold his clan and followers together, cannot throw away his weapons. With weapons still in hand, he would never think of joining ordinary people and earning an honest daily wage. So, as the means of living one day at a time, he arrives at the only road left: taking goods from citizens, with force standing behind him. Whatever the men themselves may claim, from outside no other name fits such a group but bandits. Thus they are born.

A sword is a wonderful protection against employment. Put it down and somebody might ask what useful work you can do. Keep it raised, and the questioner thoughtfully provides the answer from his own warehouse.

Places not much urbanized, beyond the Shogunate's easy reach, often became their hideouts. This town, unfortunately, had fitted the pattern.

Naturally we contacted the Shogunate and requested action. The reply was nothing at all. Not even a refusal. A refusal, at least, is a letter.

The Shogunate has no policy of leniency toward such soldiers-turned-thieves, mind you. Suppression does take place. But its strength is limited, and limited strength naturally goes first to enemies of higher danger.

Men who left office with a large army still in hand, men with popular support, men connected to foreign powers: these were marked for quick suppression. The people who had appeared in our town were none of these.

If anything, they were on the smaller side. Even so, they had enough force to make a country town shrink completely.

Too small to catch Rokuhara's attention, big enough to do banditry properly. Seen one way, we may have drawn the worst variety on the list. Chhote gunde. Small gangsters. How comforting the word small becomes when the gun is larger than anything in your hands.

Had the Shogunate been relatively stable and its army sitting idle, a clearing unit might possibly have been sent even to a town like ours. Unfortunately, this was not that time.

Rumor was spreading that Horigoe Kubo Morimasa Ashikaga would join hands with Chinjufu Shogun Yoritsuna Okabe and raise an army to topple Supreme Commander Moriuji Ashikaga. And Morimasa made no effort to explain himself, so Kamakura Central had its nerves on edge.

The three Kubo offices of Sasagawa, Oyumi and Koga, and Kamakura's central army, were all on alert for Horigoe's rising. Chasing small-time bandits was beyond them. Send any number of requests, none could pass.

Such being the circumstances, the bandit band occupying the mountain near town was enjoying an out-of-season spring.

その出自について、確かなところは誰も知らない。
　だが、推測は容易くできた。

　実の話、この手の武装略奪集団は今の大和において
珍しい存在だとは言えない。
　溢れている、とさえ言えたかもしれない。

　六波羅幕府の内外で吹き荒れる権力闘争の嵐は当然、
闘争の回数と同じだけの敗者を産み落とした。
　彼らは地位を奪われ、政治の舞台から退場する。

　だがその退場が現世から黄泉への退場をも意味する
かといえば、必ずしもそうではない。
　多くの場合その二つはセットだったが、中には粛清
の刃を逃れ、再起を期して野に潜るような者もいる。

　彼らには彼らなりの信念があったのかもしれない。
　だが市民層にとってみれば、彼らが潔い死を選んで
くれない事ほど迷惑な話も他になかった。

　何故なら彼らは、再起を期す――少なくともそう主
張して一族郎党を繋ぎ止める――以上、武器を捨てる
筈がなく、武器を手にしている以上、市井に混じって
まっとうに日銭を稼ごうなどと考えられる筈もなく、

　結果、一日一日を生きるための手段として、武力を
背景に市民から物資を奪うという道へ至るからだった。
　本人らの主張は兎も角、傍からは盗賊団以外の何と
も呼べない集団がこうして誕生する。

　幕府の目が届きにくい、余り都市化の進んでいない
地方はしばしば彼らの根城とされた。
　つまりはこの町も、そうしたケースに当てはまって
しまったのだ。

　無論、幕府には連絡し、対応も乞うた。
　だが、梨の<ruby>礫<rt>つぶて</rt></ruby>であった。

　別にこの手の賊兵に対して幕府が寛容主義を貫いて
いるという事実はない。討伐は行われている。
　だが幕府の戦力は有限であり、それは当然、危険度
の高い敵に対して優先的に向けられる。

　大兵力を有したまま下野した者、人望のあった者、
海外勢力と繋がりのある者などが、迅速な討伐の対象
となった。

I looked from the Chief back toward the bandits—and quickly dropped my eyes. The leader had happened to look this way. For an instant, our eyes met.

Arrogant. Mean underneath. Surprisingly clean-looking. Too sure of her strength. A quick collection of impressions; mostly unfavorable.

Fortunately, she did not seem to find me worth her attention. A snort, as if at my cowardice, and her interest moved on.

I let out a breath. Good. No trouble invited. By nature, quarrels did not appeal to me.

With people like this, even less. If being laughed at was the entire price, cheap only.

The Chief was gathering whoever was close by to carry out the goods. I went to help.

This work would go quickly, by the look of everyone's faces. Get the goods out, get these people gone. Not only I had understood that.

en.html:
Our Minato household was a branch of theirs. Not the usual arrangement, though, where an inheritance problem produces another household.

Five hundred years ago, it began—almost together with the senior house itself. That clan had come here on an imperial command: seal away an evil thing.

For this purpose they divided the family. One household would perform the rites to keep the evil quiet. The senior house would guard it, and keep watch over it. That separate household was ours.

Ritual families often insisted on pure blood, marrying within the family again and again. In ours, the opposite rule applied. Probably because what we guarded was something harmful.

A woman always headed our household. A husband always came from outside the district. With each generation, more outsider blood: keep the family foreign to the place, isolated together with the calamity it held.

That was also why the estate stood away from the village. High status, certainly. Belonging, no. Respect us properly, and keep us at a proper distance.

...An empty form by now, and for a long time. The senior house remained stubbornly conservative, as old ruling families tend to be. It made sure the arrangements continued. But the townspeople no longer thought as their ancestors had.

For most, our house was simply a slightly unusual local shrine. Otherwise, they would hardly have put my foster mother forward to restrain the senior house over the bandits.

Her big-sister way with people probably had plenty to do with that too. Whatever the reason, the senior house could not be enjoying any part of it.

So before going to see the Head, I did prepare myself.

We had not even reached the main subject.
My main subject, that is. He had been happily at his own all along.

To march straight in with my request would be rude. The bandits would come up anyway, so I had brought them up myself.
An excellent decision. I was regretting it thoroughly.

First some polite conversation, then the request. Simple arrangement. Only I had opened the wrong mouth. Mine had finished its work in one sentence; his was now explaining the universe, and apparently the universe was chiefly Subaru ji's fault. Beech mein kaise ghusun? Where was I to enter? A pause for breath would have done. Even the lungs seemed to be on his side. Meanwhile my request sat inside me, fully dressed, waiting to be introduced. One hour, and it had not even reached the door.

What answer could I give? I only bowed my head. From someone or other I had heard that this very old man had opposed my adoption more strongly than anyone. Now this praise. How to respond?

But he had not invented my parents' story to support his argument. Apparently, the people who had given me flesh and blood really had been like that.

They came from Narutaki in Nagasaki. The Netherlands City-State, in other words. Strictly speaking, not Yamato citizens.

Early in the 1800s by the foreign calendar, the Napoleonic Wars engulfed Europe. The British Commonwealth crushed the Kingdom of Holland out of existence. Even after the war, its territory was not restored.

News of the Dutch, left with nowhere to go, reached the Tokugawa Directorate. Relations had lasted since the government was founded. To ignore their plight now would betray the nation's good faith, it decided.

Land near Nagasaki was opened to them. An international port, already familiar to the Dutch. Merchants and diplomats stranded at trading posts across Asia came pouring in.

The Netherlands City-State, they called it. Only the Tokugawa Directorate and a few countries unfriendly to Britain recognized its independence.
A hundred years passed.

That small state in Narutaki village gradually became something other than the Dutch government-in-exile it had begun as. Europeans escaping British rule found refuge there. My ancestors had come running too.

From what I had heard, they arrived from the New World—Neo-Britain—in my grandfather's generation. Probably survivors on the losing side of the Second New World War of Independence.

Free Our America, our great homeland, from the British Empress's yoke—
Even now, they said, that slogan was whispered in the New World. Perhaps my grandfather had said it too.

...My own blood relatives. About them, so much was vague. For only a few years after my birth, I had been Jirou Arata. Arata was the family name: an ancestor who wanted Yamato citizenship had reshaped the original English surname into a Yamato one.

About twenty years ago, my Arata parents left me, still a small child, to volunteer on the continental front. Both died there. Both, I was told, had substantial Yamato ancestry as well as foreign blood. Among Narutaki families, such a story was nothing unusual.

Perhaps gratitude to the country that had sheltered them was strong. Perhaps they wanted revenge on the British Commonwealth, spreading its rule from Europe into Asia. Many Narutaki adults, women as well as men, joined the Yamato army.

Others joined the Netherlands Knights Order formed in the city-state. Four years ago, near the end of the war, it went to the Kyushu front. It fought the League forces fiercely and was wiped out.

My parents and my foster father had apparently been friends in the army. Because of that connection, he took me in.

For more than twenty years since, I had lived as Kageaki Minato, adopted into the Minato household.

Officially, the Netherlands City-State no longer existed. The League of Nations refused to recognize it and kept it under close military watch. Persecution, I had heard no report of. But life there was probably hard.

An orphan there, without parents—what would my life have been? For my foster father's kindness, how many times did I owe thanks? And to the family that had welcomed me with him.

To the Minato house, my debt was real.

〝<ruby>偉大なる故郷<rt>アウァ・アメリカ</rt></ruby>〟を<ruby>女帝<rt>ブリテン</rt></ruby>の<ruby>軛<rt>くびき</rt></ruby>から解放せよ――
　今も新大陸で密やかに叫ばれているという合言葉を、
祖父も口にしたのではないか。

　……実の親族の事は、どうにも曖昧になる。
　俺が生家の姓――大和への帰化を志した家祖が本来
の英語姓を和風に<ruby>改変<rt>アレンジ</rt></ruby>したもの――を冠し、<ruby>改次郎<rt>あらたじろう</rt></ruby>と
名乗っていたのは生後ほんの数年ばかりに過ぎない。

　およそ二十年前、<ruby>改<rt>アラタ</rt></ruby>家の父と母――二人とも大和人
の血をも濃く備える<ruby>混血<rt>ハイブリッド</rt></ruby>であったそうな――は、幼児
だった俺を残し、大陸戦線に身を投じて戦死した。
　これは長崎鳴滝の人間として珍しい話ではない。

　流亡の身を迎え入れてくれた大和の恩に報いる想い
が強かったのだろう。欧州からアジアへと支配の網を
広げてゆく大英連邦に対する復仇の意欲もあったろう。
　長崎鳴滝の成人は男女問わず多くが大和軍に参じた。

　また、市国内で結成されたネーデルラント騎士団に
加わる者も多かった。
　これは四年前――先の大戦末期に九州最前線へ出撃
し、連盟軍相手に奮戦、玉砕を遂げている。

　軍内で、俺の両親は養父と親交があったらしい。
　その縁で、養父は俺を引き取ってくれたのだ。

　それから二十年余の歳月を、俺は湊斗家の養子――
湊斗景明として生きている。

　現在、ネーデルラント市国は公的には存在しない。
　国際連盟に国家として認めない旨を宣告されたうえ、
連盟軍の厳重な監視下に置かれている。弾圧まで受け
ているとの報は聞かないが、生活環境は厳しかろう。

　そんな中で、親なしの孤児として生きる至難を想像
すれば、養父の厚意は俺にとって幾重にも感謝せねば
ならぬものだった。
　養父と共に俺を受け入れてくれた一家にも。

　俺は、湊斗の家に恩義がある。

Head lowered, answer carefully withheld, I considered what he was saying. I did understand it.

And that made my foster mother's objection clearer too.

Pride mattered. Yes. But—

A person could choose to die for it. That voluntary choice deserved respect. Another person could not impose it on them.
That, in short, would be her view.

Apni jaan, apni izzat. Your life, your pride. Spend them together if you wish. Somebody else's life, however, is not loose change for settling your own injured dignity.

And she could not say it plainly. I understood that difficulty. Speak so directly, and the Head would explode. The whole situation could go straight to the worst possible outcome.

My own mouth also had to remain shut. I could not openly agree with her; I could not join in condemning her. Silence was the only place left to stand.

The old man's angry complaints continued.

en.html:
The Head said nothing. His face twisted with anger that had nowhere to go. Terrifying.

Danger signal. Anyone who knew him well would abandon the conversation at once and retreat. Stay, and the anger would find its place to go: you.

In this district, that could ruin a person's standing here. Not one or two people had carelessly provoked him, lost their work and ended up on the street.

But leaving was not possible for me.
Hikaru had no time.

The next fit might kill her. Or the one after that. Only this was certain: it could not continue forever. The time left was probably much nearer nothing than forever.

His mood could not be my first concern now.
I bowed down to the floor.

に迷った者はかつて一人二人ではない。

　光にはもう、時間がない。

それが永遠に続くはずはなく、しかも永遠よりも無の
方にはるかに近いだろうという事だった。

　本家の機嫌を窺っているゆとりは無い。
　俺はその場に平伏した。

であれば……の話だ」景明「……は……」本家「わかるか？
　儂は愚にもつかぬ輩の妄言に乗って、湊斗
の社の清浄を汚させたりなどせぬ」本家「だが、貴様が信ずるに足る男であるならば
……意見を聞き、他国の医師に湊斗の敷居を
跨がせてもくれよう。
　儂は、そう言うておるのだ」景明「――はっ。
　して、その証は如何にして立てれば宜しい
のでしょうか」

en.html:
So I was to be tested.
Tradition, or Hikaru's life? He could not decide which came first.

I was asking him to put her life first. How much did my words weigh? On that, he meant to decide.

Wah. The life belongs to her, the illness belongs to her, but the examination is mine. Pass properly, Kageaki. Then perhaps suffering will be permitted to receive treatment.

I braced myself, body and mind.
